1058.title: What you think now
1058.hook: compare with what you wrote on day 759
1058.howItsDone: Some people who keep a journal of their practice reread old entries at the end of a season or a year, and write a short note on what they think now beside what they wrote then.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Patacara, and your line was my teachers: eight people in hard places who did the teaching. Today one more teacher comes back: the person who wrote a dated page at the start of the block on death.

A page with a date on it. Three or four lines, plain as a grocery list. On day seven hundred fifty-nine, the first day of the block on death, this path asked one question before any tradition got to speak: what do you think happens when we die? Not what you were taught, not what you ought to say. Just what came up first, even if it was a shrug, or I don't know. You dated it and put it away. Since then came Socrates and the Gita, the Buddha and the Gospels, and others besides. Today the page comes back out.
screen: `A PAGE WITH A DATE ON IT.` → `DAY 759: WHAT DO YOU THINK?` → `THE PAGE COMES BACK OUT.`

segments.voice: First, read it as if a friend wrote it. Whoever wrote those lines was honest with what they had. There's no grade on that page, and none today. Read it slowly, like a note left on the kitchen table. Second, look for small changes, not big ones. A changed mind is rarely a conversion scene. More often it's a word you'd now cross out, a fear that sits a little quieter, a picture you've added, a certainty gone soft at the edges, or a question you didn't have before. Those count. Third, a teacher on changing your mind. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor whose notebook this path has read, wrote in his Meditations that if anyone could show him he was thinking or acting wrongly, he would gladly change, because he was after the truth, and the truth never harmed anyone. The harm, he said, comes from staying in error and ignorance. Changing wasn't the failure; staying in error was. Fourth, staying put is an answer too. Some people reread their page and find they still think the same thing, only more clearly, or more calmly. That isn't a failed year. A view that has met Socrates, the Upanishads, the Psalms and a year of living, and is still standing, isn't the same view it was. It's been tested.

Ask the same question again, plainly: what do I think happens when we die? Write what comes up first under the old lines, then one more line that begins, what changed is, and if nothing changed, write that, and why.

Your line: what changed. Two honest pages, months apart, side by side. See you tomorrow.

1059.title: Still open
1059.hook: the questions this year didn't close
1059.carry: a door you know the location of
1059.howItsDone: Some people on many paths keep a written list of their unanswered questions and return to it at the end of a year, noticing which ones have changed rather than trying to close them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Meditations, and your line was what changed. Some things moved. Today is for the things that didn't settle at all.

Plenty of kitchens have one drawer for things that don't belong anywhere else: rubber bands, a key nobody can identify, the instructions for something you no longer own. You don't throw it out; you just know it's there. A year of great questions has a drawer like that too. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: some got an answer you could hold. Some got a stack of answers that don't agree, or no answer at all. Today the drawer opens, on purpose, and stays open.
screen: `A DRAWER FOR WHAT DOESN'T FIT.` → `SOME QUESTIONS DIDN'T SETTLE.` → `OPEN THE DRAWER.`

segments.voice: First, the question even the gods doubted. In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa, at the house of Death, asks what happens to a person after dying: some say he is, some say he is not. Death answers that even the gods were once in doubt about this, that it's subtle and hard to know, and offers him wealth, long life and land if he'll ask anything else. Nachiketa keeps his question. Some questions are worth more than every prize for dropping them. Second, the hymn that wonders. The Hymn of Creation in the Rig Veda asks how everything began, and ends by wondering whether even the one who watches from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps does not know. A sacred text that leaves its own question open. Third, the brother who won't sign. In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan says he can't accept a final harmony bought with a child's suffering. His brother Alyosha, who believes, answers from his own faith but doesn't walk away, and the novel keeps them both at the table. Fourth, open is not empty. These traditions have answers, and people live whole lives inside them. On this path, the answers stay in their own homes, and the choosing stays with you. A question still open at the end of the year isn't a gap in the work. It's a door you know the location of. Some people keep a list like this and look at it once a year, not to close the questions, but to see which changed shape, went quiet, or still wake them at night.

1060.title: Ahead: thinkers and practices
1060.hook: year four reads the Tao Te Ching, Montaigne, Emerson and Thoreau, and studies the science and schools of practice
1060.howItsDone: Some people who follow a reading path look over the coming year's books before they start, and pick one they are most curious about to give them something to look forward to.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was still open, and your line was a door you know the location of. Some of next year's company has carried questions like those for a long time.
screen: `A DOOR YOU KNOW THE LOCATION OF.`

segments.voice: Next year's reading list is short enough to tape to the fridge: a small old book of short chapters from China, a Frenchman writing about himself, and two Americans from the same town, one giving lectures, one building a cabin by a pond. Below them, a stack of studies on what quiet attention does to a person, and a row of doors marked Zen, Sufi, Jewish, Christian contemplative, Sikh, and more. Year four changes the shape: fewer voices, read slowly, and then the practice itself, looked at closely. Today, a look at what's ahead.
screen: `A READING LIST ON THE FRIDGE.` → `FEWER VOICES, READ SLOWLY.` → `WHAT'S AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the Tao Te Ching, one chapter at a time. It's a short Chinese classic, some chapters only a few lines long, and it keeps praising what most people overlook. Water, it says, does good to everything and settles in the low places nobody wants. The empty space inside a bowl is what makes the bowl useful. Second, Montaigne. In his note to the reader at the front of his Essays, he says that he himself is the matter of his book. No grand subject: one man, his habits, moods and fears, looked at honestly. He tries out a thought, turns it over, and isn't embarrassed to change his mind. Third, Emerson and Thoreau. Emerson, in his essay Self-Reliance, wrote: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string." His friend Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond, and wrote: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately." One wrote about trusting the inner voice; the other went to the pond to try living by his. Fourth, the science and the schools. Year four studies what researchers can honestly say about attention, habit and compassion, including what the studies don't show. Then it visits the world's schools of practice, each in its own home: Zen and Theravada, Tibetan Buddhism, Christian contemplatives, Jewish, Muslim and Sufi, Hindu, Sikh and Chinese ways, and modern secular ones. At the end, how to choose a practice, and how to respect the ones you don't choose. Year three asked what life is for. Year four asks how people have actually trained themselves to live it.

1061.title: Year three close
1061.hook: a year of great questions, answered in many voices
1061.howItsDone: Some people mark the end of a year of study by rereading their notes and choosing one question to carry into the next year, sitting with it quietly rather than trying to settle it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ahead, and your line was the thinkers, waiting next year. They can wait one more day. Today the year of great questions closes.

Gently. Live, then. Love is the practice. Work well, then rest. Let it go. Smaller, and glad. Those were the lines that closed each block this year, one for each great question: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Read them in a row and they sound almost like a life. None of them answers the question it closed. Each is more like a way of carrying it. And that is where year three ends: not with a verdict, but with a way of holding what's still unsolved.
screen: `GENTLY. LIVE, THEN. LOVE IS THE PRACTICE.` → `WORK WELL, THEN REST. LET IT GO. SMALLER, AND GLAD.` → `A WAY OF CARRYING IT.`

segments.voice: First, many voices, kept apart. On suffering, the Buddha named suffering and its cause, Job argued, and Julian heard that all shall be well. On death, the Gita spoke of worn clothes, the Gospels of resurrection, Socrates of two possibilities, without claiming to know which was true. They didn't agree, and this year never pretended they did. Each answer stayed in its own home, in its own words. Second, two pictures from a letter. A few days ago, Rilke told a young poet to love the questions themselves. In that same letter he gives two images for what those questions are like: locked rooms, and books written in a language you can't read yet. You don't break a locked door down, or force a foreign book to make sense. You live near them. Perhaps, Rilke says, one day you'll find you've lived your way into an answer. Third, loving a question isn't the same as solving it. You keep a loved question near the way you keep a friend near: you return to it, notice it has changed, and don't need it to end. Nachiketa loved his so much he turned down Death's gifts for it. Fourth, a close, not a stop. Tomorrow a new year begins, and the questions come with you. A question carried into new company tends to sound different there, the way a familiar song does in a new room. That's what this year was for: not a shelf of finished answers, but a handful of questions you know well enough to love.

If you pray, carry it into prayer; if not, let it keep you company.

1062.title: The old master
1062.hook: tradition says Lao Tzu, an archivist, wrote this book at a border gate as he left for the west; historians aren't sure he existed
1062.tomorrow: the Tao that can be told
1062.howItsDone: Taoists revere the Tao Te Ching as a sacred classic, and some readers of other backgrounds keep a copy near and read it a short chapter at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday year three closed, and your line was love the questions. Did your question come along overnight? Bring it. A new year starts today, with a small old book. Day one thousand sixty-two.

A border post on a mountain road. The guard at the gate sees an old man coming up the road, and he knows who it is: a keeper of the royal archives, a man known for his learning, and he is leaving the kingdom for good. The guard doesn't wave him through. He asks for something first. You're going away from the world, he says. Before you go, write down what you know. So the old man stops at the gate and writes. Then he walks on, and, the story says, nobody knows where he ended his days. That's the story tradition tells about the book this year opens with, the Tao Te Ching, and about the man it's credited to: Lao Tzu, the old master.
screen: `A GUARD AT A BORDER GATE.` → `WRITE DOWN WHAT YOU KNOW.` → `THEN HE WALKS ON.`

segments.voice: First, a story, not a record. The tale of the gate comes from an ancient Chinese history by Sima Qian. And the same history is honest about its own doubt: it mentions other men who might have been Lao Tzu and doesn't settle the question. Historians today aren't sure he existed at all. Some readers think the book gathered sayings from more than one hand. Taoists revere it either way. So when this path says Lao Tzu, it means the voice of the book, whoever wrote it down. Second, the word. Tao means a way, or a road. It's the path under your feet, and in this book it becomes the name for the way everything moves: rivers, seasons, people, the whole world. The book says, again and again, that this way can't be fully put into words, and then spends its short chapters trying anyway. Third, written at a gate. In the story the book isn't written in a library or a palace. It's written at a threshold, by someone halfway out the door, at the edge between one country and whatever lies past it. A gate is a strange place to stand. Nothing is kept there. Things only pass through. It suits a book that keeps praising what others overlook: the empty, the low, the quiet. Fourth, one chapter at a time. The chapters are short, some only a few lines. This year walks through them slowly, one a day, quoting the old James Legge translation where it helps and putting the rest in plain words. No hurry. The old master, in the story, wasn't in one.
screen: `A STORY, NOT A RECORD.` · `TAO: A WAY, A ROAD.` · `WRITTEN AT A GATE.` · `ONE CHAPTER AT A TIME.` · then, large: `THE OLD MASTER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit by a doorway. Find one near you: the front door, a bedroom door, even the open frame between two rooms. Sit or stand where you can see it. Notice that a doorway is mostly nothing. It's an opening, and its whole job is to let things pass. Breathe slowly and let your thoughts do the same: let each one come up to the threshold and go on through, without stopping it at the gate. If you pray, you can pray here, at the edge. If you don't, just keep watching the opening. The bell holds the time.
Tao. A way, a road, and the name an old Chinese book gives to the way everything moves, a way it says words can't fully hold. Today's word.
Your line: at the gate. Each time you walk through a doorway today, pause for one breath on the threshold, the way the old master paused before he walked on. Day one thousand sixty-two.

1063.title: The Tao that can be told
1063.word: The Tao that can be told
1063.hook: the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao; the nameless is the origin (Tao Te Ching 1)
1063.carry: not the one that can be told
1063.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching return to its opening chapter again and again, and some Taoist teachers treat it as a reminder that every description of the Way falls short of the Way itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old master wrote his book at a border gate, and your line was at the gate. Did you catch a threshold or two? Today we step through, into chapter one. Day one thousand sixty-three.

How would you describe the taste of water to someone who had never had any? Cool, maybe. Wet. Plain. Every word slides off it. Or the smell of rain on a hot sidewalk, or the face of someone you love. You can talk about these things for an hour and still not have handed them over. The words point. They don't arrive. The Tao Te Ching doesn't open by telling you what it's about. It opens by warning you that what it's about can't be fully told, and that the moment you've said it, you've already missed it a little.
screen: `THE TASTE OF WATER.` → `THE WORDS POINT. THEY DON'T ARRIVE.` → `A BOOK THAT BEGINS WITH A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name." Notice Legge's word, trodden. In Chinese the line opens with one character used twice, first as a noun and then as a verb, the Tao that can be Tao'd, and that character can mean a road and can also mean to say. Legge chose the road, a way you can walk. Other translators choose the speaking, a way you can tell. Both readings stand side by side, and the line makes sense either way: any Tao you can map or describe is not the whole of it. Second, the nameless and the named. The chapter goes on to say that, thought of as having no name, the Tao is the origin of heaven and earth, and thought of as having a name, it is the mother of all things. Two faces of one thing. The nameless is where everything comes from. The named is where we live: kitchens, cities, words for every tree. Third, both are the same. The chapter says these two come from one source and only get different names as things unfold. It doesn't ask you to throw words away. It asks you to remember that every name is a small door into something larger than the name. Fourth, the mystery has a gate. The chapter ends by calling the deepest point of this mystery a gate, the way in to all that is subtle and wonderful. A gate again. The book written at a gate opens with one.

1064.title: Beauty and ugliness together
1064.hook: when all know beauty as beauty, ugliness appears; the sage teaches without words (Tao Te Ching 2)
1064.howItsDone: In Taoist teaching, the sage's 'teaching without words' is often read as teaching by example: a teacher who lives the Way so that students learn from watching rather than from instruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter one, and your line was not the one that can be told. Did you add a silent "and more than that" to anything? Chapter two picks up right where the words ran out. Day one thousand sixty-four.
screen: `NOT THE ONE THAT CAN BE TOLD.`

segments.voice: A grandmother at a stove. She has never once given a cooking lesson. There's no recipe card, no lecture on salt. But a child stands at her elbow most evenings, watching her hands: the pinch, the stir, the way she tastes and waits and tastes again. Years later that child cooks the same dish, and the hands move the same way, and nobody remembers being taught. Some of what matters in a life gets passed on like that, with nothing said. Chapter two of the Tao Te Ching ends on that kind of teaching. But it gets there by way of beauty, and its shadow.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER AT A STOVE.` → `NO RECIPE, NO LECTURE.` → `THE HANDS REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: First, beauty makes ugliness. Legge's translation opens: "All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful." And then the catch: in knowing it, they also get the idea of what ugliness is. The moment you crown one thing beautiful, you've drawn a line, and everything on the other side of it becomes the ugly. The same goes for skill: name the skillful, and the clumsy appear. Second, pairs that need each other. The chapter lists them: what is and what isn't, hard and easy, long and short, high and low, notes and tones that make harmony together, front and back. Each half is only known by the other. Short means nothing without long. That's not a complaint about the world. It's a description of how naming works: every word comes with its opposite attached. Third, without the use of speech. So what does the wise person do, in a world of pairs? The chapter answers, in Legge's words: the sage "manages affairs without doing anything, and conveys his instructions without the use of speech." That doesn't mean lazy. It means without forcing, without the extra layer of pointing and labeling and grading. The teaching is in how the work is done. Fourth, the work stays. The chapter ends by saying the sage does the work and doesn't claim it, and because nothing is claimed, nothing is taken away. A grandmother doesn't sign the dish. It goes on being made anyway.
screen: `BEAUTY MAKES UGLINESS.` · `PAIRS THAT NEED EACH OTHER.` · `WITHOUT THE USE OF SPEECH.` · `THE WORK STAYS.` · then, large: `WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to teach one thing by example. For the next two minutes, just choose it. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you'd like the people around you to learn: patience in traffic, putting the phone down at dinner, saying thank you to the person at the counter. Now, instead of planning what to say about it, picture yourself doing it, quietly, today, with nobody told. Hold that picture while you breathe. If you pray, you can ask for help with it. If you don't, just rehearse it in your body. The bell holds the time.
Beauty and ugliness together. Chapter two's warning that every name brings its opposite with it, and its picture of a teacher who teaches without words. Today's word.
Your line: without words. Do your one thing today and don't mention it, not even once. This week closed a year of questions, crossed a gate, and went two chapters deep. Day one thousand sixty-four.
